speaker: general
text: The veterans of the ally's war are home, and the pensions they were promised are in a drawer at the treasury.

speaker: treasurer
text: The war for the ally is still on the books. Its debt is older than most of the soldiers who fought it.

speaker: organizer
text: The ally's war has a museum. Its curators still cannot agree what the last room should say.

speaker: spin
text: The ally's war is a streaming drama these days. Its sponsor wants a different ending, and has offered to pay for it.

speaker: general
text: The ally survived without us, just. Its ambassador has sent back the medal of friendship we gave it, second class.

speaker: spin
text: Our history books say we kept the peace. The ally's say we kept our distance. Both are taught to the same exchange students.

speaker: judge
text: Centuries after we stayed out, the ally's descendants want their version of it in our history lessons.

speaker: treasurer
text: The ally's heirs run the lottery that pays our pensions. They have drawn our numbers last every week for generations.

speaker: chief
text: The fields the deportations emptied have not been filled. The harvest is rotting in rows, and the farmers want someone back.

speaker: judge
text: Some of those deported were citizens. Their children, grown now, are suing for the passports they were born with.

speaker: organizer
text: The deportation lists were opened long ago. Half the country has found an ancestor on one.

speaker: spin
text: The old deportation lists are a subscription service. For a fee it will tell you whether your ancestors counted.

speaker: organizer
text: The new citizens have voted for the first time. Every party is suddenly very interested in their opinions.

speaker: chief
text: The generation given papers runs the hospitals, the farms and a third of the councils. Someone has proposed a loyalty test.

speaker: spin
text: Every family tells a story of how it got its papers. A suspicious number of the stories involve the same ancestor.

speaker: chief
text: Citizenship papers trade like antique coins, and the oldest fetch the most. Most of ours are forged in the ministry.

speaker: treasurer
text: The top rate cut is ten years old, and so is the hole it left. The growth it promised went to the people whose rate was cut.

speaker: treasurer
text: Interest on the debt from the tax cut now costs more than the schools. The lenders send a card every year.

speaker: treasurer
text: The treasury is still paying interest on the old tax cut. A child has asked the minister what it bought.

speaker: tycoon
text: The richest family still pays less tax than its gardener. The gardener has started a channel about it, with a sponsor.

speaker: tycoon
text: Since the top rate went up, three of the richest families have become citizens of a small island with a very good lawyer.

speaker: tycoon
text: The very rich have found the one kind of income the top rate forgot. It is called something new every year.

speaker: spin
text: The tax on the very rich has outlived every fortune in the country. One family means to be the first to outlast it.

speaker: tycoon
text: The very rich pay their tax to a collection firm the very rich own. It reports record compliance.

speaker: chief
text: Care for everyone is ten years old, and the waiting list is older. The nurses have asked to be paid like the promise.

speaker: scientist
text: The health service is seventy-five. It has cured two diseases and invented a third, which is the paperwork.

speaker: organizer
text: The health service is the oldest thing in the country that still works. Someone wants to sell it, for its own good.

speaker: spin
text: Care is still free after all these centuries, and the queue for it is a reality show. The winners are seen first.

speaker: chief
text: The market closed the hospitals it could not make pay. The nearest emergency room for three towns is a ferry ride away.

speaker: treasurer
text: The insurers price care by the years of life you have left. The old have noticed which way the numbers go.

speaker: scientist
text: The richest live to a hundred and forty. Everyone else has the old average, and a good view of the difference.

speaker: tycoon
text: Care has long been sold by subscription tier. The cheapest tier covers everything except illness.

speaker: organizer
text: The minimum wage has not moved since it was raised. The people on it have noticed that prices did.

speaker: treasurer
text: Machines do most of the jobs the minimum wage once covered. It is paid mainly now to the people who fix the machines.

speaker: spin
text: No one has earned the minimum wage in living memory. It is still the most argued-about number in the country.

speaker: organizer
text: The minimum wage is paid in a currency only the company shop accepts. The law was never repealed, only redeemed.

speaker: organizer
text: With wages left to employers, the delivery riders are paid by the hour, but only for the minutes they are moving.

speaker: chief
text: The average worker has two jobs now, and three is common. Turnout has fallen to the people with one.

speaker: judge
text: Wages are set at an auction every morning. The court has been asked whether a person may bid below nothing.

speaker: tycoon
text: Jobs are auctioned by the hour to whoever works cheapest. The cheapest bidder this year was a machine, bidding for its owner.

speaker: chief
text: The towers built when the zoning rules went are twenty years old. The ones built fastest have started to lean.

speaker: treasurer
text: Rents fell when the building boom came and rose again when it stopped. The towers are owned by four firms now.

speaker: scientist
text: The towers of the old building boom are listed monuments. They may not be fixed, and their tenants will not move out.

speaker: tycoon
text: The boom-years towers house a million people and no inspectors. The top floors are sold as views of the collapse.

speaker: treasurer
text: The controlled rents have held for twenty years. So have the tenants, who will not move for anything, jobs included.

speaker: chief
text: The rent-controlled blocks have waiting lists longer than a life. Places on them are being left in wills.

speaker: organizer
text: One family has paid the same controlled rent since the day it was set. Its flat is the smallest museum in the country.

speaker: tycoon
text: The controlled flats trade on an exchange. The rent is the only thing about them that has never changed.

speaker: scientist
text: The carbon price has doubled on schedule. The smoke over the old coal towns has cleared, and so have the jobs.

speaker: scientist
text: Our rivers run cooler than any around us. The neighbours' factories have moved up to the border, to breathe our air.

speaker: organizer
text: The price on carbon is so old that the smoke is out of living memory. A party promises to abolish it as unnecessary.

speaker: scientist
text: The carbon price is paid in credits the credit firm prints itself. The air has not noticed either way.

speaker: scientist
text: The gas under the valley is half gone. The refinery town has doubled, and the valley's water is tested monthly, at last.

speaker: scientist
text: The gas under the valley has run out. The refinery town has a school, a hospital and nothing left to pay for them.

speaker: scientist
text: The drilled valley sank three metres long ago. The lake that filled it is the most popular in the country.

speaker: scientist
text: The drilled valley still burns in places. The fires are a tourist attraction, with a gift shop.

speaker: treasurer
text: The tariffs are ten years old. The factories they saved have the best lobbyists in the country and the oldest machines.

speaker: chief
text: The neighbours have kept their tariffs on us since we raised ours. Who started it is forgotten; who pays is not.

speaker: spin
text: The tariff wall became a real wall, and then a tourist attraction. The factory behind it makes souvenirs of the wall.

speaker: treasurer
text: The tariffs protect a single factory these days. It makes the forms for the tariffs.

speaker: tycoon
text: Open trade made the shoes cheap and the factory towns quiet. The towns have started a party of their own.

speaker: judge
text: The trade tribunal has overruled another of our laws. It is the fourth this year, and it was about bread.

speaker: chief
text: Nothing sold here has been made here for generations. A campaign to make one thing, anything, has a waiting list of volunteers.

speaker: judge
text: The trade tribunal sits in the old chamber of our parliament, and rents it back to us on the days it is free.

speaker: organizer
text: The later pension age has filled the offices with the nearly retired. The young cannot find a desk, and the old cannot find the stairs.

speaker: treasurer
text: The later pension age saved what it promised. The treasury has found the savings, and has plans for them that are not pensions.

speaker: scientist
text: People live to a hundred and twenty and retire at a hundred. What the argument was about has passed out of memory.

speaker: treasurer
text: The pension age is a hundred and ten, and the few who reach it are paid in commemorative coins.

speaker: treasurer
text: The pension age was kept, and the bill for it has come early. The young are paying for a retirement they expect never to see.

speaker: organizer
text: The pensioners outnumber the workers now. Every election goes to whoever promises them the most and pays the least.

speaker: chief
text: The pension age has never moved, and people live twice as long. Pensioners are the largest employer of pensioners.

right.label: Leave it to the next one

speaker: spin
text: Pensions are paid out by lottery, and the pensioners are its only players.

speaker: organizer
text: The generation whose debt was cancelled bought houses, started firms and had children. The next generation borrowed it all again.

speaker: treasurer
text: The cancelled student debt was paid for by people who never went to university. They have worked out how much, to the coin.

speaker: spin
text: The day student debt was cancelled is a public holiday. The shops close, and the young cannot say what a student loan was.

speaker: organizer
text: Degrees are free and worth exactly that. The one university left sells certificates by the metre.

speaker: organizer
text: The graduates are still paying. Half of them have moved abroad to do it, and send the payments with a postcard.

speaker: treasurer
text: The student loans are finally being repaid, by graduates in their fifties, alongside their children's.

speaker: judge
text: A student loan has passed down the generations. A court is asked whether a debt can be inherited from so far back.

speaker: treasurer
text: Debts are inherited like surnames. A newborn owes an ancestor's tuition, with centuries of interest.

speaker: judge
text: The crackdown has filled the prisons with people who sold what someone else grew. The ones who grow it have never met a judge.

speaker: general
text: The drug squads have more armour than the army. The army has asked, politely, to borrow some.

speaker: scientist
text: The plant the crackdown was about is extinct in the wild. It survives in one botanical garden, under guard.

speaker: general
text: The drug squads are a dynasty. The commander's ancestor seized the first crop, and the family still sells it.

speaker: treasurer
text: The tax on legal drugs pays for the clinics now. The firms that sell them ask to advertise again, for the tax's sake.

speaker: scientist
text: Legal drugs are sold in plain packets, and the plain packets have a designer. He has made plainness very fashionable.

speaker: judge
text: A family firm has sold legal drugs since the law changed. It has applied to be a national treasure.

speaker: tycoon
text: The legal drug firms sponsor the schools, the courts and the weather report.

speaker: judge
text: The long sentences have filled every cell. The first prisoners to serve one in full are coming out, at sixty, with nowhere to go.

speaker: treasurer
text: The prisons are the largest employer in four towns. The towns have asked, politely, that crime not fall any further.

speaker: general
text: The police have long outnumbered the crimes. They patrol in pairs, looking for one.

speaker: general
text: A third of the country guards the other two thirds. The records of which third started it were lost long ago.

speaker: judge
text: The reformed prisons send fewer people back. The halfway houses are full, and their neighbours want them moved.

speaker: chief
text: Crime has fallen since the reforms. A new party says it is only hiding. Its leader was released under the reforms.

speaker: organizer
text: The last prison is a hotel. Guests pay extra for the cells, and complain about the beds.

speaker: judge
text: The halfway houses are run by the descendants of the men who once filled the prisons. They are very well run, and very dear.

speaker: spin
text: The face scanners cut street crime, and spotted three ministers where they had said they were not. Everyone wants the footage.

speaker: judge
text: The scanners' records are forty years deep. A court has been asked who owns a face, and for how long.

speaker: scientist
text: The scanners still run on every street. The footage has not been looked at in a hundred years.

speaker: spin
text: The scanners sell every face they see to whoever bids. Children are taught to walk with their heads down.

speaker: general
text: Without the scanners, the police have gone back to asking. Street crime is up a little, and so is trust in the police.

speaker: judge
text: The scanners are banned, but every phone is one. A court has been asked whether the ban covers a crowd filming itself.

speaker: organizer
text: Ours is the last country with no faces on file. Tourists come to walk down a street unrecorded.

speaker: general
text: The ban on scanners is enforced by scanners, which check that no one is carrying one.

speaker: spin
text: The law against misinformation has a waiting list of complaints. The most common complaint is about the law.

speaker: judge
text: The truth panel has ruled on forty thousand claims. It was wrong eleven times, and the eleven are now a political movement.

speaker: scientist
text: The truth panel still meets. Its oldest ruling, that the moon is not a lamp, is under appeal.

speaker: judge
text: The truth panel rules on the weather, the scores and the past. Its rulings go out before the events.

speaker: spin
text: With no law against lies, the most trusted news in the country is a man who reads the horoscopes and the election results together.

speaker: chief
text: A fake of you has given a better speech than any you have given. The polls prefer it.

speaker: organizer
text: No picture has been trusted for generations. Disputes are settled by asking the oldest person present.

speaker: spin
text: Every event has six versions and a sponsor for each. Viewers at home vote for the one that happened.

speaker: judge
text: The judges added to the highest court are retiring. Whoever sits in your chair names their successors, and the other side is counting.

speaker: judge
text: The highest court has grown with every government. It sits in a theatre now, and the judges cannot hear each other.

speaker: organizer
text: The highest court has a thousand seats and meets in a stadium. Its rulings take a season.

speaker: judge
text: A seat on the highest court is auctioned every spring. The court has ruled the auction lawful, unanimously.

speaker: judge
text: The court you left alone has struck down another of your laws. Your own side wants to know what the court is for.

speaker: judge
text: The highest court has outlived three governments that wanted it changed. It has started quoting them in its rulings.

speaker: judge
text: The highest court has nine seats, as it always had, and a waiting list of a hundred years for a case.

speaker: judge
text: The highest court still sits, alone in its building. Its rulings are read aloud to an empty square.

speaker: treasurer
text: The banks rescued with public money are profitable again. Their boards propose to remove the public's seat on each.

speaker: treasurer
text: The rescued banks have grown too large to fail again, and are behaving accordingly. The regulator has noticed nothing.

speaker: tycoon
text: The rescued banks own the treasury's building and rent it back. The rent has never once been late.

speaker: treasurer
text: The banks have been rescued nine times. The rescue has a ministry of its own, and a bank.

speaker: treasurer
text: The banks allowed to fail are gone, and the rest lend as if they remember. Small firms cannot borrow at all.

speaker: chief
text: A generation raised on the crash keeps its savings under the floor. The floors are being robbed, and the banks are empty.

speaker: spin
text: The failed bank is a museum where savers' letters are read aloud. A bank has offered to sponsor it.

speaker: general
text: Banks lost the country's trust long ago, so the militias hold the savings. The interest is paid in protection.
